articles.title: Acheter le Mac mini M6 pour l'IA locale : pourquoi c'est souvent une mauvaise idée
articles.text:
Cela fait partie de mes discussions (passionnées) depuis l’annonce du 25 août. Si on lit les promesses, on voit que le Mac mini traite les prompts LLM 4,8 fois plus vite que le M4. Avec des modèles ouverts comme Gemma 4, mais aussi les modèles chinois qui rivalisent avec ChatGPT, on se dit qu’avec 1 049 € on va enfin avoir « son IA à la maison », sans abonnement et sans envoyer ses données à qui que ce soit. C’est vrai, l’intention est bonne. Le raisonnement a juste un problème : les chiffres d’Apple mesurent la vitesse de la puce, pas la taille de ce qu’elle peut avaler. Et sur ce point, le Mac mini M6 est la machine la plus limitée de toute la gamme.
Le Mac mini M6 démarre à 1 049 € avec 16 Go de mémoire unifiée et 256 Go de SSD, soit 350 € de plus que le M4 à son lancement. La puce M6, première gravée en 2 nm, apporte 12 cœurs CPU, 12 cœurs GPU avec accélérateurs neuronaux et une mémoire configurable jusqu’à 32 Go, pas un de plus. Apple communique beaucoup sur l’IA de cette génération, et pour cause : c’est le vrai sujet de toute la gamme. Sauf qu’en lisant attentivement, les promesses de gros modèles et de cluster concernent le Mac Studio et le mini M5 Pro. Le M6, lui, hérite du discours sans hériter des moyens.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Mac Studio M5 Max-Ultra ou Mac mini M6 : peut-on vraiment remplacer son abonnement Claude ou Codex ?
            
Ce qui tourne vraiment sur 16 ou 32 Go
Oui, la machine reste capable. En 16 Go, on fait tourner correctement des modèles de 8 à 14 milliards de paramètres : gpt-oss-20b, les poids ouverts d’OpenAI taillés pour 16 Go, un Gemma 4 12B, un Qwen de classe équivalente. C’est suffisant pour transcrire de l’audio avec Whisper, résumer, traduire, classer des documents ou interroger ses propres fichiers, le tout hors ligne.
En 32 Go, on monte d’un cran avec la classe des 27 à 30 milliards : Qwen3.8-27B, multimodal et sorti mi-août, ou GLM-4.7-Flash, un petit MoE de 30 milliards dont 3,6 actifs, très à l’aise en code pour sa taille. Avec MLX, le framework d’Apple, un modèle de code de cette classe dépasse les 100 tokens par seconde sur ce type de configuration. Notre guide d’installation d’un ChatGPT local couvre tout ça pas à pas.
| Modèle | Mémoire requise | Configuration Mac mini M6 | Points forts | Vitesse attendue | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gemma 4 12B (4 bits) | 7 à 8 Go | 16 Go | Assistant généraliste, multimodal, très bon en français | Confortable, environ 20 tokens/s | 
| gpt-oss-20b (MXFP4) | environ 12 Go | 16 Go, à l’aise en 24 Go | Raisonnement, poids ouverts d’OpenAI, effort réglable | Rapide, MoE peu gourmand en calcul | 
| Whisper large (transcription) | 3 à 4 Go | 16 Go | Transcription audio de référence, hors ligne | Plus vite que le temps réel | 
| Qwen3.8-27B (4 bits) | environ 18 Go | 32 Go | Le meilleur généraliste de la classe, texte et image | 8 à 12 tokens/s, correct sans plus | 
| GLM-4.7-Flash (4 bits) | environ 19 Go | 32 Go | Code et tâches agentiques, MoE à 3,6 Md actifs | Rapide pour sa taille grâce au MoE | 
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B (4 bits) | environ 19 Go | 32 Go | Assistant de code, 256K de contexte | Très rapide en MLX, MoE léger | 
| GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek V4, Kimi K3 | 170 Go et plus | Aucune | Le modèle qui rivalise avec ChatGPT | Impossible de le lancer | 
Le vrai sujet, c’est ce qui ne tournera jamais sur cette machine. Les modèles ouverts qui font l’actualité et qui se comparent réellement aux services payants, GLM-5.3-Flash et ses 320 milliards de paramètres, DeepSeek V4 Flash et ses 167 Go de poids, demandent 170 Go de mémoire et plus. Un Mac mini M6 n’en approchera aucun, même de très loin, même en compressant à outrance. Entre 32 et 128 Go, on ne gagne pas juste en confort, on accède à une tout autre catégorie de modèles, comme on le détaillait dans notre dossier sur le nouveau Mac Studio.
Pour savoir en quelques secondes ce que votre machine peut encaisser, l’outil gratuit CanIRun.ai fait très bien le travail : il détecte votre GPU ou votre puce Apple depuis le navigateur, puis classe les modèles ouverts de S à F selon qu’ils tournent confortablement, passent tout juste ou ne rentrent pas, avec la quantification conseillée et la commande pour les lancer.
Un conseil en lisant ses résultats : ne visez jamais un modèle dont le poids frôle votre quantité de mémoire. Le fichier du modèle n’est qu’une partie de l’addition, il faut aussi loger macOS, le logiciel d’inférence et surtout le contexte, ce cache qui grossit avec chaque document ou conversation qu’on donne au modèle.
macOS refuse d’ailleurs par défaut de céder toute la mémoire unifiée au GPU. En pratique, je vous conseille de garder 25 à 30 % de marge : sur un Mac mini 16 Go, on cible des modèles de 10 à 11 Go maximum, et sur un 32 Go, on s’arrête vers 20 à 22 Go. C’est exactement pour ça qu’un fichier de 19 Go comme GLM-4.7-Flash passe bien en 32 Go et pas du tout en 24.
Trois limites que la fiche technique ne met pas en avant
Premier verrou, la mémoire plafonne à 32 Go, là où le Mac mini M5 Pro monte à 64 Go et le Studio à 128 puis 512 Go. Deuxième verrou, plus discret : la version 16 Go se contente de 153 Go/s de bande passante, les 170 Go/s annoncés étant réservés aux configurations 24 et 32 Go, facturées 220 à 440 € de plus. Or cette bande passante fixe directement la vitesse de génération des modèles. Troisième verrou, le plus important : le M6 reste en Thunderbolt 4. Le fameux cluster de Mac reliés en Thunderbolt 5 avec RDMA, celui qu’Apple met en avant pour faire tourner de gros modèles à plusieurs machines, est réservé au mini M5 Pro et au Mac Studio. Le M6 n’y participera pas, point. Ajoutez un SSD de 256 Go que trois modèles quantifiés suffisent à remplir, et le tableau est complet : cette machine est architecturalement exclue de tout ce qui fait l’IA locale ambitieuse de 2026.
Le Mac mini M5 Pro que l’on recommande à la place démarre à 1 999 €, près de 1 000 € de plus que le M6 d’entrée de gamme. Pour cet écart, on gagne 64 Go de mémoire possibles et le Thunderbolt 5 indispensable au cluster de machines. Un surcoût qui ne se justifie que si l’IA locale est vraiment le cœur du projet.
Le détail des différences avec la génération précédente est dans notre comparatif Mac mini M6 contre M4.
Face à Claude Code et Codex, le compte n’y est pas
La comparaison avec les abonnements est encore moins flatteuse. Un Mac mini M6 en 32 Go, la seule configuration réellement pertinente pour l’IA, revient autour de 1 489 €.
En face, ChatGPT Plus coûte 23 € TTC par mois avec Codex inclus, et Claude Pro environ 21 € avec Claude Code, soit cinq à six ans d’abonnement pour le prix de la machine. Et on ne compare pas des choses équivalentes.
    Pour aller plus loin
            ChatGPT Work ou Claude Cowork : lequel choisir pour automatiser son travail en 2026 ?
            
L’abonnement donne accès aux modèles « frontier » du moment, qui dépassent 80 % de réussite sur les benchmarks de code type SWE-bench, quand les meilleurs modèles locaux tenant en 32 Go tournent plutôt autour de 45 à 50 % sur les tâches agentiques. Pour du développement assisté sérieux, la différence se sent à chaque session : le modèle local propose, le modèle frontière termine. Sans compter tout ce qui vient avec : recherche Web, exécution d’outils, nouvelles versions le jour de leur sortie. Le Mac, lui, gardera sa puce et ses 32 Go jusqu’à la revente. Oui, elle est unifiée, et on ne peut pas la faire évoluer.
L’argument de la confidentialité est un sujet sérieux, mais il faut le poser honnêtement. Oui, un modèle local garde les données sur la machine, et pour des documents sensibles c’est un vrai motif d’achat. Simplement, ce motif pointe vers une machine capable de faire tourner un modèle à la hauteur de la tâche, donc vers un Mac Studio en 64 ou 128 Go, voire un mini M5 Pro. Acheter la confidentialité avec un modèle deux classes en dessous, c’est protéger des données que l’on traite mal.
La vraie vie du Mac mini M6
Le Mac mini M6 n’est pas une mauvaise machine. Il devient un mauvais achat seulement quand on le choisit d’abord pour l’IA. Son vrai terrain, c’est celui qui a fait le succès du M4 : un excellent poste de travail compact et silencieux, et probablement un des meilleurs petits serveurs domestiques du marché.
J’en sais quelque chose : un Mac mini M4 tourne chez moi en permanence, et sa journée type n’a rien à voir avec les LLM locaux. Il héberge mes projets Claude, que je pilote à distance depuis mon MacBook et qui continuent de travailler une fois le portable refermé. Il encode et décode de la vidéo 4K sans broncher. Il fait tourner mon serveur Plex avec Sonarr et Radarr. Le tout en silence, pour une consommation dérisoire, et il reste impeccable en bureautique quand j’en ai besoin. Et effectivement, même l’IA qui tourne dessus est celle d’un abonnement, la machine servant de relais toujours allumé plutôt que de cerveau.
Le M6 reprend ce rôle en mieux. Ethernet 2,5 Gigabit de série, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 et même le protocole Thread grâce à la puce réseau N1, de quoi en faire le cerveau d’une maison connectée, un serveur multimédia, une machine de sauvegarde ou un hôte Home Assistant qui consomme trois fois rien.
Et de l’IA locale d’appoint, il en fera très bien : transcription, résumé de documents privés, petit assistant hors ligne avec gpt-oss-20b. En bonus d’un achat décidé pour d’autres raisons, c’est parfait. Comme argument d’achat, c’est un malentendu. Ceux qui veulent ce profil de machine à moindre coût peuvent d’ailleurs regarder notre guide des meilleurs mini PC pour l’IA locale, où la concurrence offre parfois plus de mémoire pour moins cher.
Si l’IA locale est un projet sérieux, visez au minimum 64 Go, donc un mini M5 Pro ou un Studio, ou renoncez au matériel et gardez l’abonnement, qui reste imbattable sous 200 € de dépense mensuelle. Si vous voulez apprendre et bricoler, un Mac mini M4 d’occasion ou un mini PC de notre comparatif rend le même service pour bien moins de 1 049 €. Et si vous achetez un Mac mini M6, faites-le pour ce qu’il est : un très bon ordinateur, vendu avec une puce brillante et une histoire d’IA qui appartient surtout à ses grands frères.

articles.title: Sony attaque JBL de front avec ses nouvelles enceintes festives ULT Tower 5, 7 et Max
articles.text:
Sony attaque JBL de front avec ses nouvelles enceintes festives ULT Tower 5, 7 et Max
Sony passe à l’offensive sur le terrain des enceintes festives. Avec les ULT Tower 5, ULT Tower 7 et ULT Tower Max, la marque japonaise étoffe sa gamme ULT Power Sound de trois modèles aux formats et aux puissances variés, avec une ambition claire : venir bousculer JBL sur un marché où les basses et l’ambiance lumineuse font la loi.
Sony consolide sa gamme ULT Power Sound avec trois nouvelles enceintes festives : les ULT Tower 5, ULT Tower 7 et ULT Tower Max. Avec ces modèles, la marque japonaise entend bien renforcer sa position sur un marché particulièrement concurrentiel, actuellement dominé par JBL.
Sur ce segment, Sony s’était jusqu’alors principalement cantonné aux imposantes ULT Tower 10 et ULT Tower 9, lancées respectivement en 2024 et 2025. À en croire leur nomenclature, les ULT Tower 5 et ULT Tower 7 se positionnent donc en dessous de ces deux modèles, tandis que l’ULT Tower Max coiffe directement la gamme. Déclinées en plusieurs formats, ces nouvelles enceintes permettent à Sony de couvrir un large éventail d’usages, de la petite fête entre amis aux événements dans de grands espaces.
Des enceintes au design modernisé, sur batterie ou secteur
La plus imposante des trois, l’ULT Tower Max, fonctionne exclusivement sur secteur et vise les salles les plus vastes. L’ULT Tower 7 cherche pour sa part un compromis entre puissance et mobilité, tandis que l’ULT Tower 5 mise avant tout sur un format plus compact et facilement transportable. Ces deux dernières embarquent une batterie offrant respectivement jusqu’à 30 et 20 h d’autonomie et bénéficient d’une certification IPX4, synonyme de résistance aux éclaboussures. Toutes trois disposent d’une poignée de transport, mais seules les Tower 7 et Tower Max, plus lourdes, sont équipées de roulettes pour faciliter leurs déplacements.
Ces nouvelles enceintes ULT inaugurent également une évolution esthétique par rapport aux précédents modèles. Les éclairages, qui scintillent au rythme de la musique, sont désormais intégrés directement à la façade de leur coffret aux formes arrondies et au design plus épuré. Les haut-parleurs, bien visibles derrière leur grille acoustique, évoquent quant à eux immédiatement l’univers des enceintes de sono traditionnelles.
Usage horizontal ou vertical, dans toutes les tailles
Sur le plan acoustique, les ULT Tower 5, ULT Tower 7 et ULT Tower Max reprennent les woofers circulaires inaugurés sur les premiers modèles de la série. Associés à la technologie ULT DUCT et à un volume de charge conséquent, ceux-ci promettent une reproduction généreuse dans le bas du spectre. L’ULT Tower Max embarque ainsi trois woofers, deux haut-parleurs de médium et deux tweeters, alimentés par une amplification capable de délivrer jusqu’à 2150 W. L’ULT Tower 7 adopte pour sa part deux woofers, deux haut-parleurs de médium et deux tweeters, pour une puissance annoncée de 420 W. Enfin, l’ULT Tower 5 se contente d’un seul woofer et de deux tweeters, associés à une amplification de 300 W.
Sony indique par ailleurs que les haut-parleurs des ULT Tower 7 et ULT Tower Max sont orientés à la fois vers l’avant et vers l’arrière, afin d’assurer une diffusion plus homogène du son dans l’espace. Chaque enceinte peut également être installée à l’horizontale comme à la verticale. La technologie Sound Field Optimization ajuste automatiquement la restitution sonore en fonction de l’acoustique de la pièce. On retrouve en outre les boutons de renforcement des basses ULT1 et ULT2, déjà présents sur d’autres modèles de la gamme, auxquels s’ajoutent les nouveaux profils FLAT et LIVE.
Connectique polyvalente, chaînage audio via Auracast, etc.
Pensées pour accueillir différentes sources filaires, les trois enceintes disposent d’entrées XLR, RCA et USB-C. La diffusion sans fil passe naturellement par le Bluetooth, tandis que les amateurs de karaoké peuvent leur associer le microphone sans fil Sony ULTMIC13, proposé en option. L’application Sony Sound Connect donne accès à plusieurs réglages, notamment un égaliseur à bandes, la sélection des trois modes d’éclairage (BEAT, WAVE et MELLOW) ainsi que la gestion du chaînage sans fil avec d’autres enceintes ULT Tower de nouvelle génération.
Baptisée Party Chain, cette fonction s’appuie désormais sur la technologie Auracast, qui devrait rendre la synchronisation entre les différentes enceintes plus simple et plus immédiate. Il est également possible de constituer une paire stéréo sans fil, notamment pour concentrer la scène sonore sur une zone d’écoute précise.
Les ULT Tower 5, ULT Tower 7 et ULT Tower Max seront disponibles à partir de septembre 2026, aux tarifs respectifs de 400, 600 et 1500 €. Les deux modèles les plus compacts trouvent chez JBL des concurrentes proposées à des tarifs similaires. L’ULT Tower Max, en revanche, aura davantage à prouver face à la JBL PartyBox 720, sa concurrente la plus directe. Également dépourvue de batterie et fonctionnant exclusivement sur secteur, cette dernière est annoncée à 900 €, soit 600 € de moins que la nouvelle enceinte haut de gamme de Sony.

articles.title: Insurance companies keep pushing AI, but 98% of their adjusters' reviews on it are negative
articles.text:
Facepalm: Claims adjusters are pushing back as insurance companies put more artificial intelligence into the claims process. The tools are meant to speed up intake, sort documents, and handle simpler cases. But many adjusters say the systems are creating mistakes that workers then have to fix.
A Glassdoor analysis found that 98% of claims-adjuster reviews mentioning AI were negative – the highest rate of criticism among the occupations reviewed. Workers often complained that company leaders were pushing AI tools that did not work well and were making it harder to serve policyholders.
Ahmad Jackson saw the problem firsthand while working in the claims department at a major insurance company about a year ago. The company began using AI for initial loss reporting, the first stage of a claim when an insurer gathers details about an accident, fire, or other loss.
The goal was to move routine cases through the system faster and send difficult claims to people. Instead, Jackson said the AI often classified claims incorrectly. Adjusters had to transfer those files to the right department and deal with faulty claim summaries.
"AI is getting things wrong," Jackson told Wired. "And it's implementing more work onto the adjusters."
Jackson said he left the company and joined another carrier. He still sees uses for AI in basic administrative tasks, such as extending a rental-car reservation for a claimant. But he does not think it should be trusted with work that requires judgment or detailed knowledge of a claim.
Insurance companies are expanding their use of AI across claims operations. Customers may file a claim through a chatbot instead of speaking with a representative. Insurers can use software to review photos or videos of damaged homes and vehicles, estimate repair costs, and process uploaded receipts and records. AI tools can also summarize medical files that may run hundreds of pages.
Lemonade is among the insurers that have built their claims systems around automation. The company said its AI chatbot Jim handled initial reports 96% of the time by the end of last year. Automation handled about 55% of all claims, the company said.
Paul Staats, a Lemonade spokesperson, said AI will affect jobs in insurance and elsewhere. He said automation can allow employees to focus their "empathy, care, and expertise on the most complex claims." He also said the Glassdoor findings should be taken seriously across the industry.
The rollout comes as claims-adjuster jobs are already under pressure. The Bureau of Labor Statistics said in 2024 that it expected the number of claims adjusters in the United States to fall by 18,900 over the next decade, a 5% decline.
Employment in the sector dropped 21% between May 2025 and May 2026, according to BLS data. Glassdoor also found that entry-level job postings had fallen 50% since 2025.
Chris Martin, Glassdoor's senior economist, said AI criticism often rises when workers worry that their jobs are disappearing or when they believe a company is forcing unreliable technology onto workers and customers.
"There's no jobs, there's no good job prospects," Martin said.
The concern is not limited to job losses. Sandy Avina, a former claims adjuster and insurance consultant, said AI can make costly mistakes when it reads incomplete or poor-quality documents. A smudge on a document from an attorney, for example, can lead to a hallucination. If an AI-generated summary leaves out an important detail from a medical report, it can also result in an inaccurate payout.
In many cases, customers do not know that AI caused the problem. They may assume the adjuster made the mistake.
Geoffrey Conrad, a claims executive in Mobile, Alabama, said adjusters are tired of the steady introduction of new AI systems. "There's an AI fatigue," he said. "We're pretty much exhausted as far as the amount of AI being shoved down our throats."
Conrad said AI can be useful, but it should not be allowed to make final decisions on its own. "AI is just a tool," he said. "It should never be given the keys."
His view is shaped by his own experience as a homeowner. Before he entered the insurance business, Conrad lost his house in a fire. He said that during a crisis, policyholders need more than a computer-generated estimate based on photos.
"I needed somebody to make sure that I'm OK, my family's OK, that we're safe," Conrad said.

articles.title: Sonos introduces new Beam Ultra soundbar and Ace Ultra headphones - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Sonos has expanded the home theatre and personal listening ranges with two new products – the Sonos Beam Ultra and the Sonos Ace Ultra.
Sonos has also upgraded its audio operating system to Sonos 27.
The Beam Ultra soundbar has retained its compact design but has unlocked 7.1.2 Dolby Atmos while the Sonos Ace Ultra headphones feature an all-new driver and improved ANC (active noise cancellation).
“Beam Ultra and Sonos Ace Ultra are physical manifestations of what we mean when we say ‘sounds like Sonos’ – they combine next-gen innovation, acoustic design, and audio
engineering into something only decades of learning in real homes can create,” says Tom Conrad, CEO of Sonos.
“But the real magic happens when they take advantage of the system around them to fit your mood, whether that’s the awe of movie night, or the joy of carrying its soundtrack into your headphones the next morning.”
SONOS BEAM ULTRA – $1,099
The new Sonos midsize soundbar has nine custom built drivers including two dedicated upfiring drivers to provide 7.1.2 Dolby Atmos and improved bass.
The centre channel has been redesigned to offer clearer, crisper dialogue which has four levels of AI enhancement.
Beam Ultra can be the centre of a home theatre set up that can grow and adapt to your needs by adding a Sub or rear and surround speakers.
SONOS ACE ULTRA – $699
The latest Sonos premium over-ear headphones have been engineered with a new 40mm driver and improved Adaptive ANC that is powered by 10 microphones.
It is the first pair of headphones built on Headphone Engine 2 – a new hardware platform that allows them to link directly to a Sonos system.
With one press you can direct whatever is playing on your Sonos system and direct them to your Sonos headphones without the need to reach for your phone or an app.
The Sonos Beam Ultra ($1,099) and Sonos Ace Ultra ($699) are available to pre-order now and will go on sale on September 29, 2026.

articles.title: Authorities Turn Sality's P2P Network Against Itself, Cutting Off New Malware Payloads
articles.text:
The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) on Tuesday announced the takedown of a long-standing peer-to-peer (P2P) botnet known as Sality as part of a coordinated law enforcement operation.
The effort was undertaken on August 31, 2026, by authorities from the U.S., Bulgaria, Hungary, and Romania, in collaboration with private industry partners CrowdStrike and the Shadowserver Foundation. To that end, a peer-to-peer sinkhole operation was carried out to eliminate the threat. In tandem, Sality-linked domains have been seized in the U.S. and Europe.
"Cybercriminals, botnets, and malware are a clear and present danger to our nation's security and economy," said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. "This successful effort to take down the Sality botnet shows that by working together, the public and private sectors can be a powerful force for good."
Sality has been documented in the wild since 2003, featuring capabilities to infect and modify Windows executable files, and spread additional malicious software designed for credential theft, spam distribution, proxy services, network exploitation, and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks.
The malware is the work of a threat actor that's tracked by the broader cybersecurity community under the monikers Salty Spider, Kukacka, Sality, KuKu, SalLoad, Kookoo, and SaliCode. The group is believed to be operating out of the Republic of Bashkortostan in Russia.
Over the years, several variants of the Windows malware have been equipped with the ability to communicate over a P2P network, thereby allowing it to bypass traditional command-and-control (C2) server shutdown tactics.
One of the primary payloads delivered via Sality is EggJagger, a clipper or clipjacking tool that continuously monitors a device's clipboard for cryptocurrency wallet addresses and stealthily substitutes them with threat actor-controlled ones to redirect transactions. It's estimated that the threat actors have stolen at least $150,000 using this method.
Although Sality's operations are primarily driven by financial gain, the malware has been used to conduct three notable DDoS attack campaigns, highlighting the threat actor's willingness to repurpose the botnet for personal or political purposes, CrowdStrike said. The attacks targeted -
- Arabic Financial Forum ("forex2030[.]com") in April 2016
- Ukrainian Forum ("kharkovforum[.]com") in February 2022, a day after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine
- AvanChange in September 2023
Sality has been distributed through various methods, including infected network shares, USB devices, file sharing, compromised websites, email attachments, and P2P networks, effectively creating a self-propagating botnet that regenerates new infections without requiring any active efforts from the threat actor.
In July 2022, operational technology cybersecurity company Dragos revealed a campaign that targeted industrial engineers and operators to seize control of Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and co-opt the devices into the Sality botnet.
According to CrowdStrike, the botnet is said to have allowed the operator to distribute malicious payloads to more than 15,000 infected machines worldwide, adding that two independent P2P networks, known as version 3 and version 4, remained active until the disruption occurred.
"They shared the same codebase and were operated by the same threat actor, but used incompatible protocol versions and different cryptographic keys," the CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations said.
The takedown operation involved turning Sality's P2P architecture against itself to isolate all peers in the network from the threat actor's control and neutralize their ability to communicate with infected machines. This, in turn, prevents them from receiving payload download instructions or payload transfers, rendering the botnet ineffective.
"The same properties that made Sality resilient also created the conditions for its undoing," CrowdStrike explained. "Sality's P2P protocol cannot be patched. Unlike conventional malware that can receive code updates from a C2 server, Sality's spreading mechanism is a file infector: it propagated by attaching itself to executables on disk."
The counterattack leveraged an approach called peer list manipulation, which was also used in the 2014 GameOver Zeus and 2017 Kelihos botnet disruptions. It took advantage of the fact that Sality bots blindly trusted the P2P network without verifying who was added to it.
As long as a machine was publicly reachable and responded correctly to the P2P handshake, it was accepted as a legitimate peer. This factor, coupled with the lack of authentication, cryptographic identity, or allowlist, meant that "anyone" could join the network as a full participant with no way to distinguish it from a genuinely infected host.
The peer list manipulation technique, as the name implies, involves tampering with the peer list, a data structure containing a finite set of known super peers, which are publicly reachable infected machines that serve as the basis of the P2P network. The botnet checks whether its stored peers are still online every 40 minutes. Peers that respond to the check accumulate reputation, while those that fail lose reputation and are eventually purged.
This maintenance cycle is abused to remove legitimate peers from the network via protocol-level manipulation during peer verification and insert purpose-built sinkhole entries into the emptied peer list.
"The disruption targets super peers first, as they form the network's communication backbone," CrowdStrike said. "Once isolated, both URL packs and file packs stop propagating. The majority of infections sit behind firewalls or network address translation (NAT) and cannot be directly contacted."
For these machines, a more passive approach is adopted. When they contact the sinkhole nodes during their normal maintenance cycles, their peer lists are purged, leaving them permanently isolated.
The coordinated operation, besides sinkholing the P2P network, also took down the URLs that have been found to host Sality payloads. In doing so, it prevents the malware from downloading these files and retrieving additional payloads. The list of URLs is below -
- theunforgiven.p8[.]hu/img/top.gif
- painelwebradiodigital.awardspace[.]info/v3/readme.pdf
- sgwebdesigner.free[.]fr/left.gif
- www.yonelco[.]com/icon.png
- pozdravizbeograda[.]com/readme.pdf
- highclass.atspace[.]com/styles.gif
- situluimihai.3x[.]ro/top.png
- gatheredovertime[.]com/nb4
- imagebucket[.]biz/nv4
All Sality-infected machines are now configured to beacon to CrowdStrike-operated sinkholes. Organizations are recommended to review network logs and endpoint telemetry for UDP traffic to the "lighthouse" IP address "188.166.101[.]148." Any match indicates a Sality infection that requires remediation.
"This operation demonstrates that P2P architecture, long considered a shield against disruption, is not invincible," CrowdStrike said. "With sufficient technical investment, precise understanding of protocol behavior, and coordination with law enforcement and industry partners, even the most resilient criminal infrastructure can be dismantled."
"While the disruption prevents new payloads from reaching infected machines, existing malware already installed on those systems remains active and should be removed."
The joint crackdown is one of the key pillars under President Donald Trump's Cyber Strategy for America. Referred to as "Shape Adversary Behavior," it aims to identify and disrupt malicious networks, scale national capabilities, and alter adversary calculus by degrading their tools and infrastructure.
"This unique collaboration among international law enforcement and private sector partners only enhances the FBI's cybersecurity capabilities and our efforts to neutralize the threat posed by the Sality botnet," said Patrick Grandy, the Assistant Director in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI) Los Angeles Field Office.
"The FBI will continue working with our partners to prevent further cyber-enabled attacks and theft from victims in the United States."

articles.title: Espionnage industriel : Apple accuse OpenAI de détruire les preuves
articles.text:
Le 31 août 2026 restera dans les annales de Cupertino comme le dernier jour de Tim Cook aux commandes, quinze ans presque jour pour jour après avoir succédé à Steve Jobs. John Ternus, patron de l’ingénierie matérielle depuis des années, prend le fauteuil ce mardi 1er septembre, avec une keynote calée dès le 9, où les iPhone 18 sont attendus. Le même lundi, les avocats de la firme déposaient devant le tribunal fédéral de Californie du Nord une pièce de plus dans le procès qui l’oppose à OpenAI depuis le 10 juillet, et cette pièce a un nom : le MacBook de Chang Liu.
Ce que le MacBook d’un ex-ingénieur a livré aux avocats d’Apple
Pour ceux qui auraient raté les premiers épisodes, la plainte déposée le 10 juillet vise OpenAI, io Products (l’entité matérielle issue du rachat de la société de Jony Ive) et deux anciens de la maison. Tang Yew Tan d’abord, vingt-quatre ans chez Apple et désormais responsable du matériel chez OpenAI, puis Chang Liu, ingénieur systèmes senior parti en janvier après huit ans de service. Apple reproche à Liu d’avoir conservé un MacBook professionnel encore relié à ses réseaux, puis d’avoir exploité un accès résiduel et un bug d’authentification pour télécharger des dizaines de fichiers confidentiels. OpenAI conteste tout, qualifie la plainte d’« étrangement personnelle » et en demande le rejet, en soulignant au passage qu’Apple n’avait tout simplement pas coupé les accès de son ancien salarié.
Le document déposé lundi ajoute un chapitre que Cupertino qualifie de « preuves choquantes ». Les avocats de Liu ont fini par remettre le MacBook qu’il utilisait depuis son départ, après des semaines de retard selon les écritures d’Apple, et une première analyse forensique en a tiré quatre constats. Liu aurait non seulement téléchargé un schéma de circuit confidentiel, mais s’en serait servi dans son travail chez OpenAI, via une simulation lancée en mars dans LTspice, un logiciel d’ingénierie électronique très répandu. Son accès persistant à un espace de stockage en ligne utilisé par Apple aurait été connu d’autres personnes chez OpenAI. À l’annonce d’une enquête interne le visant, il aurait envoyé à une collègue des instructions pour effacer des éléments, instructions qu’elle aurait confirmé suivre. Il aurait enfin utilisé un outil portant le même nom qu’une application interne d’Apple. Le tout reste une allégation, le document est en partie caviardé et la collègue en question n’est pas identifiée dans les passages rendus publics.
Un secret avalé par une IA peut-il encore être rendu à son propriétaire ?
Dans un procès pour violation du secret des affaires, la boîte à outils du juge est connue depuis des décennies : ordonner la restitution des documents, interdire leur usage, faire détruire les copies. Le cas Liu complique l’affaire d’une manière assez inédite. Dans des messages de la même période, l’ingénieur expliquait que son « agent » d’intelligence artificielle avait appris à lancer LTspice et à en analyser les résultats. Apple en tire un argument central : une information confidentielle ingérée par un agent ou un modèle qui apprend de ses entrées peut engendrer des usages irréversibles et qui se propagent en continu. Un secret industriel dans un modèle, c’est une goutte d’encre dans un verre d’eau, on ne la récupère pas à la pipette. D’où l’insistance de la firme pour obtenir une procédure de collecte de preuves accélérée et une injonction préliminaire, deux demandes qu’OpenAI combat pied à pied.
John Ternus, ingénieur de formation et vingt-cinq ans de maison, hérite d’un contentieux qui porte exactement sur des schémas, des cartes mères et des prototypes. Plus de 400 anciens salariés d’Apple ont rejoint OpenAI, qui prépare un appareil grand public avec les équipes de Jony Ive, et c’est ce même appareil que la plainte vise en filigrane. Sa première keynote, le 9 septembre, devrait dévoiler le premier iPhone pliable, si les rumeurs disent vrai. Tim Cook, devenu président exécutif du conseil, gardera un œil sur le dossier, mais les décisions sur la suite reviendront désormais à un ingénieur.

articles.title: Dardo de Sony a jugadores: si eres un "consumidor razonable", ya sabes que tus juegos digitales de PlayStation no son tuyos
articles.text:
Sony está en lucha con el público no solo por la muerte de los juegos de PlayStation físicos, sino también por las condiciones de venta de los digitales. En su respuesta a una demanda por el funcionamiento de la PlayStation Store y el sentido de propiedad de los títulos que se venden allí, la compañía argumentó que es una obviedad que los juegos digitales no les pertenecen a sus compradores.
De acuerdo con Sony, cualquier "consumidor razonable" sabe que lo que se compra al interactuar con la PlayStation Store son licencias para acceder a los juegos, y no los juegos en sí mismos. La demanda contra la compañía se presentó en junio y sus impulsores sostienen que la tienda en línea infringe las leyes californianas, puesto que da a entender a los usuarios que están comprando algo, pero que en realidad solo lo están licenciando.
En su respuesta ante la justicia, la empresa dijo que el acceso a licencias y no a los juegos en sí mismo está explicado de forma clara en los términos y condiciones de la plataforma. Pero no se limitó a ello, sino que planteó su propia lógica: si no se vendieran licencias, solamente un comprador podría obtener acceso a los juegos digitales de PlayStation.
"En la era digital, no es plausible alegar que los consumidores razonables creyeran que estaban adquiriendo la 'propiedad' de un juego digital. Si ese fuera el caso, entonces el demandante Edward Heycock no habría podido obtener el juego Resident Evil Requiem el 25 de febrero de 2026 por $69.99 de PlayStation Store después de que el demandante Jason Mendoza hubiera obtenido Resident Evil Requiem el 14 de febrero de 2026, porque el Sr. Mendoza, no Sony, habría sido el propietario en ese momento", argumentaron desde la compañía.
Sony se defiende de la polémica por la distribución de juegos digitales de PlayStation
Así las cosas, Sony defiende el funcionamiento (y el negocio) de la PlayStation Store sosteniendo que sería imposible distribuir juegos digitales si no fuera por medio de un sistema de licencias. Lo que plantea la compañía tiene lógica, pero ello no necesariamente invalida el reclamo de muchos jugadores que tal vez no está reflejado en la demanda en cuestión.
La decisión de Sony de matar los juegos físicos de PlayStation desde 2028 ha despertado un sinfín de interrogantes respecto de un futuro solo con lanzamientos digitales. Si el jugador no es realmente dueño de la copia de los juegos que compra, eso significa que tarde o temprano se le puede negar el acceso a los mismos sin que tenga opciones para evitarlo.
Si bien Sony está respondiendo a una demanda puntual sobre la distribución de juegos digitales de PlayStation que han presentado cuatro jugadores, muchos otros usuarios tienen preocupaciones genuinas sobre el futuro de sus bibliotecas personales. Disminuir esas dudas al concepto de ser o no "consumidores razonables" puede sentirse como una subestimación innecesaria.
Guste o no, el futuro de la distribución de juegos de PlayStation es 100 % digital y se pondrá en marcha desde 2028. Una decisión que no solo acaba con la propiedad real sobre tus títulos favoritos, sino que también se carga el mercado de segunda mano que la propia Sony alguna vez celebró.

articles.title: IKEA lance des têtes thermostatiques Matter à seulement 15 euros - Numerama
articles.text:
Ikea veut devenir un acteur de référence dans la maison connectée. Sa stratégie : casser les prix et rendre la concurrence absurde, notamment en attaquant toutes les catégories. Après avoir lancé des ampoules, des prises, des stores et des capteurs, le Suédois s’attaque au secteur du chauffage.
La LILJEBAGGE, une tête thermostatique connectée pour radiateur à eau chaude, est apparu à la fin du mois d’août dans le catalogue d’IKEA. Elle est listée à 199 couronnes sur le site suédois et à 14,99 euros en Allemagne. Aucune date n’a été communiquée pour la France, mais la saison de chauffe arrive et Ikea a rarement pour habitude de réserver des produits à des pays.
15 euros chez IKEA, 60 à 90 euros chez Tado, Netatmo ou Eve
Si vous n’êtes pas familier avec le principe d’une tête thermostatique connectée, il s’agit d’un composant qui remplace la molette vissée sur le robinet d’un radiateur à eau chaude et qui pilote l’ouverture de la vanne, pièce par pièce, selon une programmation horaire. Le LILJEBAGGE peut augmenter ou diminuer l’ouverture d’un radiateur pour viser une température ciblée par l’utilisateur.
La proposition d’IKEA est très basique : sa tête thermostatique n’a que deux boutons (plus et moins), un petit écran qui s’allume uniquement quand on touche l’appareil, un réglage par demi-degré et une autonomie de 18 mois avec deux piles AA. Il n’y a ni géolocalisation, ni détection de présence, ni apprentissage des habitudes : l’utilisateur règle une température dans l’application.
IKEA vise donc un public avec un faible budget qui souhaiterait connecter plusieurs radiateurs. Une tête Aqara, Tado, Eve Thermo ou Netatmo se négocie entre 50 et 90 euros pièce et il faut souvent ajouter une passerelle propriétaire vendue séparément. Pour équiper cinq radiateurs, on passe d’environ 400 euros à 75 euros. À ce niveau de prix, IKEA joue dans une catégorie différente. L’entreprise a quand même quelques rivaux autour des 30 euros, mais il ne s’agit pas de grandes marques connues pour leur fiabilité.
Côté protocole, la tête LILJEBAGGE communique en Matter over Thread, ce qui lui permet de rejoindre Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, SmartThings ou Home Assistant sans passer par la passerelle Dirigera d’Ikea : il faut un Apple HomePod ou un Google Home à la maison pour communiquer avec les radiateurs.
Des risques sur la fiabilité du protocole : ne pas avoir de pont est un risque
Attention aux apparences : le fait de se passer d’un pont n’est pas forcément une bonne chose. Dans les faits, le Thread reste le maillon faible de la maison connectée. Le protocole a besoin d’un routeur Apple/Google/Amazon quelque part pour fonctionner… mais est soumis à de nombreuses instabilités que n’a pas le protocole Zigbee. Quand un accessoire Thread décroche, il n’y a pas de bouton de redémarrage : il faut souvent le délier, le réinitialiser et recommencer.
Depuis le basculement de son catalogue vers Matter fin 2025, IKEA enchaîne les retards, les ruptures et surtout les problèmes d’appairage. Ikea a reconnu publiquement des problèmes de jeunesse sur certains réseaux domestiques : Matter n’est pas encore la technologie parfaite promise par ses concepteurs. C’est pour cette raison qu’une approche comme celle d’Aqara, avec des appareils qui communiquent en Zigbee à un pont qui s’occupe de la liaison Matter, nous semble aujourd’hui plus solide. IKEA simplifie tout, mais prend le risque de créer des dysfonctionnements.
Dans quelques années, la présence de têtes thermostatiques connectées pourrait être rendue obligatoire. Le décret n° 2023-444 impose un système de régulation automatique de la température pièce par pièce dans tous les logements. L’échéance, initialement fixée au 1er janvier 2027, a été repoussée au 1er janvier 2030 pour le parc existant par un décret publié fin décembre 2025, tandis que le neuf reste sur 2027. Des millions de foyers français vont devoir s’équiper.
Une régulation pièce par pièce permet de ne pas chauffer une chambre vide toute la journée et de programmer le retour à température avant le réveil ou le retour du travail. L’ADEME estime qu’un degré de moins sur le thermostat représente environ 7 % de consommation de chauffage en moins sur la saison. À 15 euros la tête, l’investissement est amorti en une seule saison de chauffe, à condition que l’appairage tienne.

articles.title: German SpaceTech HyImpulse secures over €50 million to accelerate Europe’s sovereign launch capabilities | EU-Startups
articles.text:
HyImpulse Technologies, a Neuenstadt am Kocher-based manufacturer and system provider of commercial rockets for suborbital and orbital launch services, today announced a Series A Extension round of more than €50 million in equity.
The round was co-led by JOIN Capital and Ace Capital Partners, with participation from new investors, including North Ventures, BW-Capital, Bayern Kapital and the German Aerospace Centre (DLR), alongside continued support from existing shareholders, including Campus Founders Ventures. 
In October 2025, the company announced it had raised €15 million in equity capital as part of its Series A funding round and secured an additional €30 million in financing. The extension round brings the company’s total equity and public funding to more than €125 million.
Dr. Christian Schmierer, co-founder and CEO of HyImpulse, said, “This financing reflects our investors’ confidence in our team, technology and commercial vision. Europe needs sovereign, responsive and economically sustainable launch capabilities. Our proprietary hybrid propulsion technology and suborbital and orbital services position us to meet growing demand across commercial, institutional and defence markets.”
HyImpulse was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) by Dr. Schmierer, Dr. Mario Kobald, Konstantin Tomilin, and Ulrich Fischer. Headquartered in southern Germany, HyImpulse is a launch services company that develops and provides suborbital and orbital launch capabilities based on a proprietary propulsion technology.
The company’s mission is to open access to space by delivering affordable, reliable launch and in-space services. Its proprietary hybrid propulsion technology combines non-explosive paraffin fuel with liquid oxygen and claims to offer a safe, cost-efficient and scalable alternative to conventional kerosene-based systems.
The German firm also notes that its lower system complexity and reduced component count enable safer, more responsive launch operations and competitive launch economics.
HyImpulse already operates a commercial suborbital platform, the suborbital launcher SR75. Following its inaugural flight campaign at the Koonibba Test Range in South Australia in 2024, the company is preparing its next SR75 launch from SaxaVord Spaceport in Scotland.
HyImpulse’s SR75 and its broader suborbital roadmap targets offer launch capabilities of up to Mach 15 and ranges of up to 10,000 kilometres. According to the company, this addresses growing demand from government agencies, research organisations and defence customers for hypersonic testing, threat simulation, and suborbital flight services.
The company reports that it is capitalising on growing demand for independent launch capabilities, with an order book exceeding €350 million across its suborbital and orbital programmes.
“Europe doesn’t just need more rockets; it needs launch economics that actually work. HyImpulse has built a fundamentally leaner rocket architecture: roughly half the parts, a path to half the cost per kilogram and far less capital required to get to orbit. They have already proven the technology in flight. That’s why we co-led this round, and why the upcoming SR75 launch matters,” said JOIN Capital Founding Partner Jan Borgstädt.
The company plans to use this funding to accelerate development and commercialisation of HyImpulse’s launch services portfolio, including the second SR75 launch from SaxaVord Spaceport by the end of 2026 and the maiden flight of its launch vehicle SL1.
It also intends to expand production capabilities and scale commercial operations across Europe and beyond. It will also strengthen the company’s position in key growth markets, including dedicated and responsive satellite launch services, in-space mobility, and suborbital research and defence applications. It has over 100 employees at locations in Neuenstadt, Ottobrunn and Glasgow.

articles.title: How this Vancouver artist helped bring Canada to life in Marvel's Wolverine
articles.text:
It’s rare for Canada to play itself in games. It’s even rarer for Canada to play itself in big-budget games.
That’s why Canadians were excited to see North Vancouver featured so prominently in gameplay footage from the next PlayStation blockbuster, developer Insomniac Games’ Marvel’s Wolverine. Not only does it give an oft-unseen representation of Canada in gaming, but it also pays tribute to Wolverine’s Canadian roots. (It’s also not the only Canadian location players will visit, as creative director Marcus Smith teased to us.)
And while Insomniac is based in Burbank, California, a veteran Canadian artist has been spearheading the studio’s Canadian representation in Marvel’s Wolverine. Enter Gavin Goulden, senior art director who’s worked on the likes of Irrational’s BioShock Infinite and Insomniac’s Sunset Overdrive and Marvel’s Spider-Man series. The Halifax native now lives in Vancouver, giving him a particularly strong personal connection to ol’ Canucklehead’s latest gaming adventure.
MobileSyrup sat down with Goulden to learn more about the journey to bring Canada to life in Marvel’s Wolverine, the differences of working on Spider-Man vs. Wolverine, how his art has evolved across several games and the advancement of technology, and more.
For people who might not be aware, what does your job as senior art director entail? What does that work look like on a day-to-day basis for Marvel’s Wolverine?
Gavin Goulden: My day-to-day work is really focusing on the team to make sure that we have a consistent visual style on the project. So part of that is fulfilling the player fantasy and having that in every aspect of the game. But it’s also working with a team of leads and a team of artists to make sure that we’re delivering the highest quality we possibly can.
With Marvel’s Wolverine, a lot of people are really excited because this is a Canadian character, and we get to finally see him in Canadian locations in a game of this scale. But we don’t often see that in media. It’s alluded to sometimes, like in X-Men: Origins Wolverine, there’s that fun bit, “Serve your country!” “I’m Canadian.” Or even in Deadpool and Wolverine, we see the CN Tower behind them. But Marvel’s Wolverine is the biggest example of this kind of Canadian representation. So where did that inspiration come from? How did those whole discussions begin in terms of bringing Canada into the game?
Goulden: As everyone knows, Wolverine is Canadian — possibly the most famous Canadian superhero there is, though Wolverine will never call himself a hero. But we felt it was really important to have him in his home country. So when we picked Vancouver, it’s a little different than what comic fans might be used to, but we also knew that we could do Canada justice because Canada rarely gets to play itself. Vancouver, especially, doesn’t get to play itself, so usually it’ll be New York or something like that. But it’s very rare that Vancouver is Vancouver, and being able to represent that was extremely important.
And honestly, it was a cool opportunity to be able to give a place that I love justice. We did a lot of research. It’s kind of in my backyard, so it’s not a ton of research I need to do, but wanting to show like the sulphur pile, which is an iconic landmark in Vancouver… It also gave us room to have a fantastical version of Vancouver, too. And then also, as you’ve seen, getting the Squamish signs, the Sea-to-Sky Highway, and having that be a familiar yet cool Marvel experience, too.
Once you decided that Vancouver would be featured in the game, how did you decide on those specific elements, like the sulphur piles, to include?
Goulden: It was essentially, “How can we place Wolverine in a location that would support the more brutal combat?” So not wanting to be downtown and slicing through a bunch of people and causing chaos in that way. But it’s also a good segue, as you saw in the gameplay trailer, of going from a location to a motorcycle ride. So that location geographically fit the gameplay beats that we wanted to set up.
As someone who is actually not only Canadian but living in Vancouver now, what are you hoping to convey about the city or Canadiana as a whole to players? Especially Marvel fans who aren’t from Canada or aren’t familiar with Vancouver.
Goulden: Wanting to pay respect to a very beautiful location in the world. Part of it’s also breaking a stereotype. Again, since you rarely get to see the city itself or the location itself. So getting to see the authentic version of it might help maybe inspire people to come pay a visit. You can even do that drive in real life. I do it all the time. So hopefully, [we’ll] get some people in to see how beautiful it is in real life.
Is there anything that you were particularly jazzed about getting to include?
Goulden: The wording on the signage, driving up the Sea-to-Sky Highway, is very authentic to British Columbia. Since the Olympics when we added the Squamish translations of the words. So having that small detail, if people can pick up on that, I feel super happy about it. It’s a very, very specific detail that is important to me.
Looking at your job as a whole… A lot of people are very excited when they see authentic, hand-drawn art nowadays — they really respond to that human touch. What goes into making good art direction?
Goulden: A lot of it is conveying the emotion and the gameplay beats that you want in the game. So art really serves gameplay in that way, and trying to sell how you’re intended to feel in cinematics and when you’re in the fight. So in order to make that happen, we do a lot of pre-planning, a lot of concept work, colour scripts, mood boards, stuff like that, to get people all on the same page. That’s really the main thing: getting everybody looking at the same thing and wanting the same goal. So throughout the project, you have to hit all those beats, then also make sure that everything’s consistent so that one mission doesn’t look wildly different from the other and that it’s a very balanced, cohesive feeling project.
Insomniac has made three Spider-Man games now, and Wolverine inhabits the same universe, but obviously, it’s in its own pocket of it. When you’re coming into Wolverine, how did you want to differentiate that from Spider-Man, which is a similar sort of photorealistic visual style, but obviously Wolverine’s more of a gritty character. How did you go about approaching making Wolverine feel similar and something that could realistically co-exist with Spider-Man, but also be its own distinct thing?
Goulden: Totally. While they share the same universe, 1048, and they are kind of based in the same world, so to speak, Wolverine is a much more gritty, brutal, violent character. The world he belongs in is violent, and he’s a violent weapon, so to speak. So that contrast between him and Spider-Man was super important. I’d also say that Spider-Man is my childhood hero, but Wolverine is the hero of my adolescence. So being able to kind of translate that in my career has been a really cool experience. Because you’re going from the “Friendly Neighbourhood Spider-Man” to the living weapon of Wolverine. And I think we showed that difference through brutal combat, being very ferocious and stuff like that is super important and a great opportunity between the two.
I imagine as an artist, as a game developer, working on these beloved Marvel characters is a little bit of a double-edged sword in the sense that on the one hand they’re very beloved, and it must be an honour to work on that. But then there’s a lot of pressure that comes with decades and decades of lore and fandom behind these characters. So when you’re approaching designing for Spider-Man or Wolverine, how do you strike that balance of drawing from comics or other media, but also finding that sort of distinct “Insomniac stamp” on it?
Goulden: What we always want to do is pay respect to the past, but carve our own path into the future. There’s literally decades and decades of comics and history that we can pull inspiration from, which we do. But ultimately, we want to make our own Wolverine. We want to make our own Spider-Man. We want our take on it. And when we’re doing that, we think about, “Well, what’s important for the character?” And that’s visually, too. “What are landmarks that everybody is familiar with on character designs or locations that you’d have?” And while those still say true, our take on it can become our unique twist. So I wouldn’t necessarily say there’s a lot of pressure or anything. Really, we just want to do right by the character and by the fans that they appreciate the new take on Wolverine.
I was listening to an earlier interview you did where you were talking about Spider-Man and the unexpected amount of work that goes into all of the costumes that he has with him being such an agile character. Obviously, Wolverine’s a different character with his own distinct qualities — he’s sort of getting shred to pieces in combat, with his costume breaking and the blood and gore and all that. Were there any particular design challenges or specific things to Wolverine that you had to work around and overcome?
Goulden: I wouldn’t necessarily call them challenges; they’re kind of opportunities. But the difference between Wolverine and some of the things you would gather from the interviews from Spider-Man is that Wolverine, like you said, can get torn up. He has his healing factor where he’s healing, and that’s a new element for us, completely. Being able to carve into a character and then have it regenerate was totally new technology that we had to develop. Beyond that, it’s also body hair. [laughs] We haven’t had to render such a hairy character before, and we did it very well. Running at 60 frames per second with strand-based hair all over his body is a feat.
I actually wanted to ask about the body hair! People were really taken aback by just how detailed that was. It’s kind of a funny, full-circle moment for Insomniac because I remember there’s that great running gag in Spider-Man.
Goulden: Where he’s got three chest hairs? [laughs]
Yeah! And then you zoom in, he’s actually got three chest hairs, and now you’re doing a character —
Goulden: That has a few thousand more? [laughs]
So, I’m curious: How much work goes into the tech and design of having a lifelike, realistic body hair system?
Goulden: It’s a ton of work, and it’s between our artist and our core rendering team. Much smarter people than I am. But it’s a totally new approach to it, and it took a lot of trial and error to get it right. It’s generally new, so I can’t really get into a ton of details about it.
Playing the demo a few weeks ago at Insomniac, I really liked the different visual styles there are. When you’re going into Level 3 Rage Mode, it’s this sort of black-and-red coat of paint on the world. And even when you’re skulking around, there’s that visual element of this ephemeral blue highlight on their skeletons, which I thought was a really cool approach to “Detective Modes” in games. How did you land on how you wanted these heightened visual elements to be represented?
Goulden: Every mode needs to be distinct and register with players immediately. But then there’s also inspiration that we take from the source. So for Rage, a lot of inspiration came from “Black, White, and Blood,” the comic run. And while we didn’t go literally with that, that is the foundation of why it looks that way. So when Wolverine enters Rage, all he’s thinking of is the target, “Who am I going to fight? Who am I going to take down?” And by embracing that source, what does the gameplay need to be? We can kind of marry those two together so that the world goes black and white. It doesn’t matter. All that matters is the target.
And then for the circulatory system that you’re talking about, you’ll see red trails and stuff in Madripoor. Those are all senses. “How do you visualize Wolverine’s animalistic super senses?” And it’s we have to do it visually so that people know. Obviously, just saying that you smell something isn’t really compelling or easy to understand, so that’s sort of our translations. “How would Wolverine be able to detect a person?” He’d hear their heartbeat. “How do we visualize a heartbeat?” You show it through our ethereal kind of rendering on the character, and you have their heart pumping as you get closer to them.
I believe you’re coming up on 20 years in the industry, correct?
Goulden: I think a little over 20, actually! My very first job was doing pixel art on Motorola V300. I can barely remember it. [laughs]
That’s awesome. How has the evolution of technology over this time informed your approach to art direction in games?
Goulden: The technology changes our workflow, but at the end of the day, it’s always about heart and conveying what emotional beats are and what the gameplay beats need to be, and then using art to best sell that and make it engaging for players. So, while we’ll be able to do muscle simulations, we can render all the hair and it looks beautiful, it’s really just a tool that helps those foundational skills. So the foundation is always the same, whether it’s pixel art or super high-end rendering.
Part of what I think everyone loves about Insomniac is the sheer variety of the games that you make. You can have something that’s more cartoonish, colourful, like Sunset Overdrive or Ratchet & Clank, but then you can have something more “realistic” like Spider-Man and Wolverine. Tracing the evolution between Sunset, Spider-Man, and now Wolverine, what were some of the biggest lessons that you learned from those previous games that you’ve brought into Wolverine?
Goulden: That’s a great question. I think every project ends up having different challenges that you need to address. So with Wolverine, compared to something like Sunset, which is more, I would say, playful and alive — Wolverine is more grounded and brutal and realistic. And I think the lesson that I have learned is that art serves the project the most. So whatever the project needs, art is there to complement that and present it in the best way possible for players. And as I advanced from pixel artist, character artist, lead character artist, art director — that becomes more clear because it’s less about me and my team, and it’s more about the company and the project. So how does art play this big role to make the game a success?
What’s it been like to return to Canada after working at all of those studios in the U.S.?
Goulden: It’s great. I had lived in the States for, I want to say, 12 years or so. Definitely feeling homesick every time I’d come back to Vancouver — getting a tattoo worked on, usually in Squamish, actually. So every time I’d come back, it would just be a reminder of like how much I missed Vancouver. Insomniac became a remote-first company, so that was a great opportunity for me to move back. I took it, and no regrets. I love being back in Vancouver.
I also think a lot of people will be really jazzed to learn that one of the art directors at Insomniac on Wolverine is Canadian. It’s a great story.
Goulden: It’s crazy. Getting to work on Wolverine as a Canadian, and then getting to portray the place you love in that same game? It’s probably one of the proudest things I’ll ever get to do in my career, getting to show a place I love in digital form as itself. How many opportunities do you get to do that?
Marvel’s Wolverine releases exclusively on PS5 on September 15.
For more on the game, check out our full hands-on preview and interview with creative director Marcus Smith.

articles.title: Your future is in Virginia
articles.text:
Is this the future of America?
Massive AI infrastructure is being built out across the US. But if you want to know what the data center occupation looks like, visit Loudoun County, Virginia, where that future arrived 20 years ago.
by Lauren Feiner
Photos by Stephen Voss
In 2007, the US was on the cusp of an economic recession, and Buddy Rizer was tasked with finding Loudoun County, Virginia, a new way to make money. Rizer’s earlier career as a radio DJ didn’t exactly make him an obvious candidate to find a solution, but he was looking for what he called a “real job” and stumbled into a role at Loudoun’s economic development authority.
This new gig came with urgency thanks to the bursting of the housing bubble: More than 80 percent of the county’s revenue came from residential real estate. The goal, at the time, was to raise the commercial tax base from about 19 percent of revenue to something like 23 percent, Rizer recalls. Today, just over half of the county’s tax revenue comes from commercial sources. To jumpstart that turnaround, Rizer turned to the carcasses of another recent bubble burst — those of the dot-com era.
The county had been home to the headquarters of AOL, which by 2000 was the US’s largest internet provider. Combined with its proximity to the nation’s capital and access to resources including water and electricity, Loudoun quickly emerged as the physical manifestation of the internet, the place responsible for how the majority of Americans got online. Estimates suggest that as much as 70 percent of the planet’s internet traffic passed through Loudoun County.
But after the collapse of dot-com stocks in 2000, followed by AOL’s disastrous merger with Time Warner, much of that industry dried up, and Loudoun was left with hulking, empty buildings and miles of fiber optic cable already laid in the ground. Where some people saw abandoned infrastructure, Buddy Rizer saw opportunity: “And so I thought if we can fill those, that would be a good start,” he says. Rizer soon realized that the same factors that made Loudoun County attractive to AOL could once again make it a hot spot for technology. It still had an internet exchange point, lots of land, a government eager for investment, and a capable local electricity utility. “And so we came up with this plan to attract data centers.”
Today, Loudoun County has another moniker: Data Center Alley. Over just a small portion of its roughly 515 square miles, it’s home to about 250 data centers, the densest concentration in the world. For a long time, residents there recall only a passing understanding of this, if they realized it at all. The development of data centers in Loudoun was just something going on in the background of many residents’ lives. They noticed construction along main roads, paid an increasingly lower property tax rate, and sent their kids to coveted public schools.
The county’s data center boom arrived as tech companies expanded into the cloud, a sanitized name for the blocky buildings that house rows and rows of servers. And with that business came prosperity: 22 new schools built in just the last 15 years, tax revenue from data centers alone that exceeded the county’s operational budget by $35 million in 2024, and a decline in real property tax rate for residents from about $1.29 to 80 cents per $100 in assessed value since 2008.
Some longtime residents never heard of their county’s nickname until recently, when the effects of data centers on the community started to become impossible to ignore. What had been a relatively quiet boon locally was starting to foment a national backlash elsewhere, and starting to disturb daily life in Loudoun, too.
The current, massive US data center buildout has been accelerating thanks to the widespread adoption of generative AI, which has created a growing need for the physical infrastructure to run tremendous amounts of “compute” — the industry term for processing power. There are already 3,000 data centers in operation around the US, according to an April analysis by the Pew Research Center, with 1,500 more in development. When Rizer began recruiting companies to build data centers in Loudoun, he sat on conference panels for secondary markets. Now when he attends data center conferences, Loudoun is the biggest market there, and “there’s more economic developers than there are data center companies, because everybody sees the opportunity.”
Loudoun County residents are also starting to take notice. Within the past few years, data centers have been elevated from an unremarkable part of daily life in Loudoun to something that many residents now think about every day. For some, it’s the constant hum they hear from their decks; for others, it’s the transmission towers that loom over their favorite green space, or the surprise call from their energy utility that one of those towers could go up in their own backyard. While residents recognize that data centers have brought a lot of prosperity to the county, they’re beginning to wonder how much more they can take.
As communities around the country begin recognizing the potential opportunities of building data centers, the efforts have also faced immense pushback. Opposition to this development is shaping strange alliances across the political spectrum and has become a central issue in this year’s midterm elections. New York and Texas have begun pumping the brakes on new data center buildouts, worried about how their energy grids could support them without leaving residents stuck holding the bag if major tech players change plans. Local stories from around the country show that residents are coming out to community meetings in droves to oppose data centers. In at least one case, a violent attack on a local Indianapolis official appeared motivated by his support for data centers. And national polls show that many Americans do not want to live near them.
With its long history hosting data centers, Loudoun residents have more recently taken to calling it something new: the canary in the coal mine of data center development. Want to know what the country’s future looks like? Loudoun County’s past gives a strong glimpse of it.
Even in Loudoun, where the existence of data centers has been a fact of life for nearly two decades, Rizer says that in the last few years, community opposition has become more vocal. “Before then, people understood what we were doing,” he says. These days, residents seem more aware of the inconveniences.
Rizer is no stranger to this kind of response to his projects, but the tone of the pushback is different. Residents have always had myriad worries: economic, environmental, and aesthetic. That part isn’t new. “I’ve done $70 billion of deals here, and the only thing in common is that somebody’s been against every single one of them,” Rizer says. “I have never seen, in my entire career, the vitriol, the hate that is associated with this.” Asked to put his radio DJ hat on to choose a soundtrack for this moment, he chuckles and says the first one that jumps into his head is Taylor Swift’s “You Need to Calm Down.”
As Rizer and other officials in Loudoun field their own residents’ concerns about data centers, they’re also being flooded with calls from local officials across the country looking for their advice. Rizer is the first to admit that hosting a data center, let alone hundreds, is not the right choice for every community. He stands by the work he’s done to bring them to Loudoun, and still believes they’ve benefited the county on the whole. But data center expansion in Loudoun has recently taken on a life of its own, to the point that even Rizer no longer spends his time courting new facilities. “We don’t want more data centers here, but we want those that are here to be successful and continue to contribute to our community,” he says, diplomatically.
But new facilities are coming anyway, and even Rizer, the “godfather of data centers,” is powerless to stop them. Over a series of visits to Loudoun County, I wanted to see for myself what it’s like to cross through communities surrounded by the cloud. Is the data center future that so many across the country seem to fear all it’s been built up to be?
“I have never seen, in my entire career, the vitriol, the hate that is associated with this.”
Long before it became Data Center Alley, Loudoun County was already solidifying its role as the hometown of the modern internet. In 1996, AOL decided to move its headquarters from neighboring Fairfax County to Loudoun, eventually employing more than 5,000 workers in Ashburn at its peak in 2004. Soon, the first internet exchange point, MAE-East, would make a similar move to Ashburn, making Loudoun the physical location where much of the world’s internet traffic flowed. It was further solidified as a tech juggernaut when telecom company MCI WorldCom also opened a large office in the area, which became its headquarters in 2003.
The companies brought more than just jobs and a new workforce to the area. They also laid fiber underground across the county, attracting other tech firms to the area because of the convenient promise of low latency and proximity to the nation’s capital. The attention earned Loudoun nicknames like “the Silicon Valley of the East” and “Dulles Technology Corridor,” after the nearby airport.
For a while, AOL and MCI’s presence made Loudoun an unlikely but bustling tech hub. Between 1990 and 2000, the county population doubled to 170,000. Early AOL employees have recounted lavish parties thrown by the company in its heyday, including “go-go-style dancers” and a sushi conveyor belt around an airplane at the nearby annex of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum.
During this time, data centers were already starting to pop up in Loudoun County, but with little fanfare. The first one arrived in 1997, and after that there was a slow drip of new data centers permitted in the area. In 2000, the local zoning administrator made a decision that would have lasting consequences later on, but made little noise at the time. Because data centers looked similar to offices, they became designated as “office parks,” meaning that they could be built on any land zoned for office space “by right” — bypassing more time-intensive regulatory review. That meant that unlike other commercial facilities like heavy machinery plants, which face more restrictions being built near populated residential areas, data centers could be built wherever offices had been allowed.
Then the dot-com bubble burst. In early 2000, AOL announced a blockbuster merger with Time Warner for more than $160 billion. But as the first wave of internet companies suffered sharp declines, AOL’s ad revenue tanked, and the country’s largest provider of dial-up internet was soon undercut further by the rise of faster cable broadband. MCI filed for bankruptcy in 2002 after a major accounting scandal. By 2006, it was acquired by Verizon, and a year later, a much diminished AOL announced it would move its headquarters to New York.
Soon after came the financial downturn that became the Great Recession. Looking for unique ways to pitch the county, Rizer, then a newly minted business development manager, saw an opportunity in the recently emptied buildings and miles of fiber still lacing Loudoun’s roads. From 2002 to 2005, no new data centers had been permitted. In the years after Rizer began courting them, only a few were permitted per year, county data shows, but growth was slow and steady. Then, in 2014, the number of data centers permitted jumped to seven. Rizer recalls feeling like the county could finally start relying less on its taxes from residents and more on commercial revenue. “We were catching up on schools and catching up on salaries for our workforce,” he says. He recalls no pushback out of the ordinary on any development project, and says that for 15 years, “everybody loved the data centers because of the difference it made in our community.” In 2018, data center permits tripled to 21 in a year, and they reached a new peak in 2022 at 25.
Only those who were really paying attention seemed to notice that Loudoun was quickly becoming the data center capital of the world. Many longtime residents I spoke to sheepishly admit they hardly recognized Loudoun’s global reputation for data centers, though they perhaps passively noticed the new, blocky buildings that popped up along main roads or the tall transmission towers near their favorite running trail.
Over the past 20 years, though, Loudoun residents have seen a direct impact of data centers on their lives, whether they knew it or not. Real property tax rates declined dramatically, while property values have gone up in some communities as much as 182 percent in the last decade, even at residences close to data centers, according to county officials. The county has paved smooth roads and built sprawling athletic fields, a recreation center with an Olympic-size pool, and an average of nearly one and a half state-of-the-art public school buildings every year for the past 15 years, all thanks largely to the revenue generated by the county taxes data center companies have to pay anytime they get new equipment. And while data centers have gotten a reputation for creating relatively few jobs once they’re constructed, the county says that for every job inside those buildings, three and a half non-construction jobs are “supported” throughout the rest of the state economy. Those include ongoing maintenance at data centers, like electricians or HVAC technicians, and employment at other tech companies that move to Loudoun to be near where the data lives.
While the data centers take advantage of a long-standing tax exemption from the state, Rizer emphasizes that the county has never spent a dime to attract them to the area. “A majority of the people that live here now only know prosperity, only know the strongest local economy in the country, only know great services and great schools,” Rizer says. “And so they don’t necessarily connect to that. They don’t see that common thread between the fact that the data centers are here and they have a great quality of life.”
My most recent visit to Loudoun is on a July day when wildfire smoke that’s wafted down from Canada has sent air quality into a Code Purple. The ashy filter makes the grayish buildings all around look especially drab, though when I visit a local bike trail lined with trees and transmission towers, I still see plenty of cyclists braving the AQI that exceeds 200 in some spots.
Julie Bolthouse, a longtime Loudoun resident who grew up across northern Virginia, drives me by the old AOL campus and points out a building with a playground on the other side of the street. “That used to be a major daycare center here in the heart of Data Center Alley, because there were so many people who worked here,” she says. “Now it’s just these big, giant computer energy-guzzling, water-guzzling warehouses.”
The lot where the old AOL campus sat is now filled with construction equipment and several-story buildings. The old headquarters has been demolished to make way for — you guessed it — more data centers.
Throughout Loudoun, Bolthouse remembers land that now houses data centers being home to business centers and dentist’s offices. She returned to the area after college, enjoying that it made an easy trip to both DC and Virginia’s Shenandoah National Park, and feeling comfortable in an area that’s generally not prone to major weather events like hurricanes. In 2017, the organization she joined, Piedmont Environmental Council (PEC), began tracking the impact of data centers on the local environment. A year later, Loudoun’s Board of Supervisors had one of its most contentious votes ever, narrowly approving a 750,000-square-foot data center spanning over 100 wooded acres near Goose Creek. Groups like PEC loudly objected to the development over environmental concerns, while those in favor of the proposal argued development would happen there regardless; it was just a matter of what would get built.
“Everybody loved the data centers because of the difference it made in our community”
Today, Bolthouse is the director of land use at PEC and helps lead a coalition of Virginia groups that advocate for stronger protections, tracking, and transparency around data center development. Bolthouse isn’t dispositionally anti-data center, nor does she want to see existing ones in the area torn down or shut off. But she does advocate for a pause on new development. “This industry is kind of creating a narrative that they’re up against communities, and that there’s a community backlash, and we just need to explain to the communities the benefits of data centers,” she says. “But what they’re really up against is physics. They’re up against the reality of what it takes to build out gigawatts of power, and the impact of building out gigawatts of power has direct impacts on people.”
Recently, she’s found, more of her neighbors are paying attention. She recalls 2025 as a turning point, where PEC no longer had to do the legwork to get people invested, but instead was triaging which press requests would make the most impact given its limited capacity. And for residents, data centers were becoming more than just eyesores. They were beginning to disrupt life in Loudoun.
Vicky Hu lives in a red brick home on a cul-de-sac beside a peaceful, tree-lined stream. Her backyard stretches far along the water, where a white gazebo gives shade to sit and watch the deer she says regularly cross her yard. Including her mother and daughter, three generations of Hu’s family have lived in this house.
